Projects.subtitle: ESP32 designs for audio, control and local AI. Explore the code, connections and documentation for each project.

btdac.moment: BTDAC receives Bluetooth A2DP audio and sends it over I2S to the PCM5102 DAC. Its line output can connect to an amplifier or powered speakers.
btdac.struggle: The firmware keeps a BLE control channel separate from audio. The Android app can find the device, connect and request test tones. The project guide covers wiring, DAC configuration and power.
whatWorks: Bluetooth A2DP audio reception
Stereo I2S output to the PCM5102
BLE connection from the Android app
Test tone generation through the tone: command
RGB LED indicating connection and playback states
whatDoesnt: The line output requires an amplifier to drive passive speakers
The app controls test tones; remote volume and equalization are not implemented
Battery life depends on the cells and power consumption; no reference measurement has been published

bom.notes: Two compatible cells for the 2S pack

specs.label: Power supply
specs.value: 2S pack and 5 V regulator; see the wiring guide

speaker.moment: WiFi Speaker combines network and Bluetooth audio reception on an ESP32. Two MAX98357 I2S amplifiers drive the audio channels, and an LCD shows playback status.
speaker.struggle: The firmware includes WiFi radio, URL streaming and Bluetooth A2DP modes. The web interface lets you select sources and adjust controls. The project is still in development; external services and stream addresses can change.
whatWorks: WiFi radio and URL streaming modes in the firmware
Bluetooth A2DP reception
I2S output to two MAX98357 amplifiers
Web control interface
LCD and mDNS name access on compatible networks
whatDoesnt: Streaming requires an accessible network and audio source
YouTube integration depends on an external Invidious instance
Battery life and usable power depend on the build; no reference tests have been published

resources.name: Random Nerd Tutorials - ESP32 Web Server

bom.notes: Two compatible cells for the 2S pack

futureFeatures: Streaming and reconnection validation across different networks
Power consumption and battery life measurements

hios-node-ai.moment: HIOS Node AI connects an ESP32-S3 to an Ollama server on the local network. Pressing a button sends a preset text query and displays the response on an OLED screen.
hios-node-ai.struggle: A FreeRTOS task handles the HTTP request while the main loop updates the display. The model runs on the server, not the ESP32. The WiFi network, server address and model name are configured in the firmware.
whatWorks: Preset query sent to Ollama’s /api/chat endpoint
Physical button to trigger the query
Status and response shown on an SSD1306 OLED display
HTTP request handled in a FreeRTOS task
HTTP error and WiFi disconnection indications
whatDoesnt: Requires an Ollama server accessible on the local network
The query and credentials are configured before compilation
Voice capture, audio playback and TinyML are not implemented in the current firmware
Response time depends on the server, model and network

specs.label: Interaction
specs.value: Physical button and preset text query

pad.moment: HIOS PAD organizes keyboard shortcuts, media controls and mouse actions in layers. Ten action keys, two ALT keys, an encoder and a joystick let you select and run actions with an on-screen reference.
pad.struggle: USB and Bluetooth BLE carry HID actions. WiFi is used for configuration, updates and communication with the companion. This optional program sends computer status to the PAD and enables features such as system-wide microphone mute.
whatWorks: Keyboard, mouse and media actions over USB and BLE
Layers and groups navigable from the display
Joystick mouse control and layer-dependent encoder actions
JSON configuration and a web editor in the companion
Computer status and system-wide mute through the companion
PAD-hosted web interface with virtual controls and basic editing
whatDoesnt: Actual computer status and system-wide mute require the companion and a network connection
The companion has Windows and Linux providers; macOS is not implemented
The direct web interface has tests with a simulated device; applying changes on hardware still needs validation
Firmware battery measurement is disabled; its former GPIO is used for the NeoPixel

specs.label: Inputs
specs.value: 10 action keys, 2 ALT keys, encoder and joystick

specs.label: Network
specs.value: WiFi for configuration, OTA and companion

futureFeatures: Validation of changes applied through the device’s direct web interface

calculators.intro: Calculators for electronics, construction, weather and everyday tasks. Calculations run in the browser.
steps: Choose a calculator from the list, grouped by category.
Adjust the sliders or enter numbers; results update automatically.
Start from a template or save a named configuration in this browser.
Copy the summary for results as text, or copy a link containing your configuration.
calculators.tip: In the resistor calcs (LED, RC filter, ADC divider), the 'E-series' control snaps the value to the nearest commercial one (E12/E24).

composer.intro: Create a chiptune composition, listen in the browser and export it.
steps: Choose a track and instrument. Click the grid to add notes; drag to move or resize them.
Set the tempo and number of bars, then start playback. Enable the loop to repeat it.
Export a MIDI or WAV file, or copy a share link containing the whole composition.
To play on compatible hardware, export the device format and load it through the device web interface.
composer.tip: Hardware playback requires firmware compatible with the exported format. The final sound also depends on the device and its audio output.

guitarTuner.intro: Tune guitars, basses, ukuleles and bowed strings using reference tones or microphone input. Audio analysis runs in the browser.
steps: Pick your instrument and tuning, and set the reference A4 if needed.
Click a string to hear its reference tone.
Start the mic and play a string — the matching string lights up and the needle shows how far off you are.
guitarTuner.tip: The default A4 reference is 440 Hz. Adjust it to match the reference used by your ensemble or recording.

resistorColorCode.intro: Read a resistor value from its color bands, or find the bands for a value.
steps: Pick 4 or 5 bands.
Set each band's color.
Read the resistance and tolerance.
resistorColorCode.tip: Five-band resistors use three significant digits. The final band indicates the tolerance.

ohmsLaw.intro: Solve Ohm's law and power: enter any two of V, I, R, P and get the rest.
steps: Type exactly two known values.
Leave the other two empty.
Read the computed results below.
ohmsLaw.tip: P=V·I, V=I·R, plus the derived forms P=I²·R and P=V²/R are all applied.

httpStatusCodes.intro: Look up any HTTP status code, its category and what it means.
steps: Type a code (e.g. 404) or a word (e.g. teapot).
Scan the filtered table.
Use the color tag to read the class at a glance.

asciiUnicode.intro: Inspect any character or code point in decimal, hex, octal and binary.
steps: Type a character, or a code point as 65, 0x41 or U+0041.
Read its formats and name.
Browse the control-character table below.
asciiUnicode.tip: Works with emoji and other astral-plane code points, not just ASCII.

noteFrequency.intro: Convert between musical note, frequency and MIDI note number.
steps: Set the A4 reference (default 440 Hz).
Enter a note, a frequency, or a MIDI number.
Read the matching values and cents offset.
noteFrequency.tip: Cents show how far a frequency is from the nearest equal-tempered note.

ipv6Expand.intro: Expand an IPv6 address to its full form or compress it to the canonical short form.
steps: Paste any IPv6 address.
Read both the expanded and compressed forms.
Copy whichever you need.
ipv6Expand.tip: Compression follows RFC 5952: lowercase, longest zero-run collapsed to ::.

hmac.intro: Calculate an HMAC from a key and message in the browser.
steps: Pick an algorithm (SHA-1/256/384/512).
Enter the secret key and the message.
Copy the hex or base64 MAC.
hmac.tip: Unlike a plain hash, HMAC mixes in a secret key to authenticate the message.

csvJson.intro: Convert CSV to JSON and back, with proper RFC 4180 quoting — fully local.
steps: Choose a direction (CSV→JSON or JSON→CSV).
Paste your data and pick the delimiter.
Copy the converted output.
csvJson.tip: With the header row on, CSV rows become objects keyed by the first row.

patterns.intro: Explore JavaScript patterns with editable examples that run in the browser.
steps: Choose a lesson.
Read the explanation and edit the code.
Run the example and review the console output.
patterns.tip: Examples run in a frame isolated from the page. This isolation does not block network requests made by the code.

notes.intro: Write Markdown notes with a preview and storage in this browser.
steps: Create a note and give it a title.
Write markdown on the left.
See the rendered preview on the right.
notes.tip: Use notes for formatted text and code snippets for examples organized with tags.

mermaid.intro: Create diagrams with Mermaid syntax and a live preview. You can export an SVG or share the diagram through a URL.
steps: Pick a template or write your own diagram code.
The preview re-renders as you type.
Export the SVG or copy the share link.
mermaid.tip: It runs with securityLevel strict — no scripts or click actions in diagrams.

textDiff.intro: Compare two blocks of text line by line in the browser.
steps: Paste the original on the left.
Paste the changed version on the right.
Read the +added / −removed lines below.
textDiff.tip: Use this tool for text changes and the object comparator for structural differences in JSON.

regex.intro: Test a regular expression against text, see matches/groups and preview a replace — all local.
steps: Write the pattern and flags (g, i, m, s, u, y).
Paste the test text.
Inspect matches and groups; try a replacement.
regex.tip: Use the g flag to get every match; named groups show up alongside numbered ones.

uuidUlid.intro: Generate UUID v4 (random) or ULID (sortable, time-prefixed) IDs locally.
steps: Choose UUID or ULID.
Set how many to generate.
Copy one, or copy all.
uuidUlid.tip: ULIDs sort lexicographically by creation time — handy for keys/logs.

encoder.intro: Convert text to/from Base64, base64url, hex or URL encoding — fully local.
steps: Pick a mode and direction (encode/decode).
Type or paste the input.
Copy the output, or send it to another tool.
encoder.tip: base64url is the URL-safe variant used in JWT — no +/ and no padding.

hashDigest.intro: Calculate a text hash in the browser.
steps: Pick an algorithm (SHA-1/256/384/512).
Type or paste the input text.
Copy the hex or base64 digest.
hashDigest.tip: When comparing hashes, use the same algorithm and text encoding for both inputs.

snippets.intro: Save code snippets in this browser or in your account.
steps: Enter a title, optional tags and the snippet content.
Save it: without signing in, it is stored in this browser; when signed in, it is stored in your account.
After signing in, use the import option to copy local snippets to your account.
snippets.tip: To share a snippet by link, save it in your account and make it public. Local snippets are imported only when you choose to do so.

payload.intro: Format and inspect JSON in the browser. Share links include the data in the URL.
steps: Paste or type JSON into the editor.
Use Prettify / Minify and the path explorer to navigate it.
Click “Share link” to copy a URL that reproduces this exact payload.
payload.tip: The link includes the complete JSON. Check for passwords, tokens and other data you do not want to share.

typeChecker.intro: Check whether a JSON value is assignable to a TypeScript type, fully in the browser.
steps: Define your interfaces / types in the type panel.
Set the root type name to validate against.
Paste the JSON value and press Check to see diagnostics.
typeChecker.tip: Load the example to see a passing case, then tweak the JSON to watch diagnostics appear.

jwtPlayground.intro: Decode, sign and verify JWTs (HS, RS, ES) in the browser.
steps: Paste a token to decode the header and payload instantly.
Switch to Encode to build and sign a new token.
Use Verify with the secret or public key to confirm the signature.
jwtPlayground.tip: For RS/ES, you can generate a demo key pair to test signing and verification.

dnsLookup.intro: Query DNS records (A, AAAA, MX, TXT, NS, CNAME) over the network.
steps: Enter a domain name.
Pick the record type you want to query.
Read the resolved records; change the type to compare.
dnsLookup.tip: TXT records are where SPF, DKIM and verification tokens usually live.

certificateCheck.intro: Query a site’s TLS certificate to review its issuer and validity dates.
steps: Enter the hostname (no https:// needed).
Run the check.
Review the expiry date and the risk indicator.
certificateCheck.tip: Check the expiry date when planning a certificate renewal.

objectToTypes.intro: Generate TypeScript interfaces from a JSON example.
steps: Paste a representative JSON object.
Set the root interface name.
Copy the generated types into your codebase.
objectToTypes.tip: Types are inferred from the supplied data. Review optional fields and other possible values before using them in your application.

randomString.intro: Generate random strings with a configurable length and character set.
steps: Choose the length and character set / options.
Watch the live entropy estimate.
Copy the generated value.
randomString.tip: Entropy is an estimate based on length and character set. Requirements depend on how the generated value will be used.

objectCompare.intro: Compare two JSON objects and spot structural differences fast.
steps: Paste the left and right objects.
Use Swap if you mixed them up.
Read the highlighted differences.
objectCompare.tip: Great for diffing an API response before vs after a change.

siteChecker.intro: Check URLs periodically through network requests from your browser.
steps: Add the URL you want to check.
Allow notifications if you want alerts.
Keep the tab open for periodic checks.
siteChecker.tip: Monitoring stops when the tab closes. An opaque response does not reveal the HTTP status, so it cannot confirm that the site is working correctly.

tokenEstimator.title: Token and context estimator
tokenEstimator.description: Explore an approximate split of text into fragments. This tool uses a heuristic, not a model’s tokenizer.
tokenEstimator.placeholder: Enter or paste text to explore its fragments.
tokenEstimator.modelReference: Model reference (does not change the estimate)
tokenEstimator.ratioHint: Ratio between this heuristic’s fragments and the words in the text.
tokenEstimator.empty: Enter text to see its fragments.
tokenEstimator.scope: The actual count depends on the tokenizer and conversation format. This view uses simplified rules that do not change when you select another model reference. The memory example applies a fixed coefficient and does not represent a model’s KV cache. To plan context and memory, use the tokenizer and measurements of the engine you intend to run.

grammar.title: Command formats for hardware
grammar.description: Define the response format with JSON Schema or GBNF. Validate each command before using it to control hardware.
grammar.scope: Grammars constrain the format in compatible engines; they do not guarantee that a command is correct or authorized. Validate structure, values and permissions before running actions. Code examples use English names and prompts and need adapting to your device and engine. The receiver snippet only illustrates actions for desk_lamp; it does not implement every profile or include the validation of a complete application.

voiceLatency.title: Voice latency estimator
voiceLatency.description: Compare scenarios by adding end-of-speech detection, transcription, network, first-token and speech synthesis times. These are illustrative values, not product measurements.
voiceLatency.scope: Measure each stage on the target device and network. This calculator adds times sequentially; it does not run speech recognition, synthesis or audio playback.
voiceLatency.streaming: Streaming can overlap stages. To evaluate it, measure when audio starts and how the response continues, as well as the total time.
voiceLatency.tuning: End-of-speech thresholds and chunk size affect waiting time and phrase boundaries. Adjust them using representative recordings and tests.
voiceLatency.done: Simulation complete; no audio was generated.
voiceLatency.hintFast: The sum is below half a second. The actual experience needs measurement of the complete system.
voiceLatency.hintMedium: Compare each stage’s contribution to identify where to reduce the wait.
voiceLatency.hintSlow: The sum approaches or exceeds one second. Compare these durations with device measurements.
voiceLatency.hintLong: Check which stage contributes the most time. This result describes the scenario, not a performance measurement.

vram.title: Memory scenarios for local models
vram.description: Compare sizes and formats with a simplified formula. Profiles are illustrative scenarios; they do not describe an exact model architecture or guarantee that it will load.
vram.offload: GPU layers assigned in the example
vram.partialBody: The formula assigns {gpu} of {total} layers to GPU and {cpu} to CPU. It estimates {ram} GB of RAM. Check actual usage when loading the model.
vram.cpuTitle: The scenario assigns layers to RAM
vram.cpuBody: The formula totals {total} GB of weights and cache and allocates {ram} GB to RAM. Change context or format to compare.
vram.ramTitle: The calculation exceeds the specified RAM
vram.ramBody: The result is {needed} GB against {available} GB specified. This is not a load test or a measurement of your computer.
vram.scope: Weights are approximated as parameters × bits / 8. The cache uses a fixed coefficient of 0.0003 multiplied by context and model size, adjusted by the format factor; it does not use the actual architecture. The calculation reserves 0.6 GB for the engine. Results let you explore this formula, not select hardware or confirm compatibility. Adapt file names, models and command options, then measure usage with your engine.

esp32Bridge.title: ESP32 code for querying Ollama
esp32Bridge.description: Generate firmware that queries Ollama and displays the response on an OLED screen. The HTTP request runs in a FreeRTOS task.
esp32Bridge.defaultPrompt: Respond in English, directly and concisely, in two sentences.
esp32Bridge.codeHint: Starting point to adapt in PlatformIO or Arduino IDE
esp32Bridge.scope: networkTask sends the HTTP request while loop() handles the button and display. Check the pins, core assignments and dependencies for your board. The example waits for WiFi at startup and does not include a complete reconnection or task synchronization strategy. Code comments and status messages are in English. Test it on your build before integrating it; it does not guarantee a refresh rate or eliminate connection errors.

showcase.title: PAD in use
showcase.description: The display brings together the active layer actions and device controls. These examples show how the same PAD fits different parts of your day.
showcase.imageAlt: Photograph of PAD in Editing mode with copy, paste, undo, redo and media controls.
showcase.caption: Actual prototype photograph in Editing mode. Layout and labels can change with firmware configuration.

editing.title: Editing and navigation
editing.body: Assign copy, paste, undo and redo to the keys. Switch the encoder between scrolling and zoom, and use the joystick to move the pointer.
editing.requirement: USB or BLE HID actions; no companion required.

meetings.title: Control a meeting
meetings.body: Use Meet, Zoom or Teams layers for microphone and camera shortcuts. Add the companion to toggle global mute and receive the actual microphone state.
meetings.requirement: Shortcuts depend on the active application; global mute and feedback require the companion.

media.title: Playback and volume
media.body: Control playback and volume with the keys and encoder. With the companion, PAD receives the computer volume to display it on screen.
media.requirement: Media controls use HID; displaying actual volume requires the companion.

pad.title: PAD software: controls, editor and companion
pad.description: Configure PAD actions and organize them by context. The firmware provides USB and Bluetooth controls; the companion adds web editing and communication with Windows or Linux.

controls.title: Layers, shortcuts and mouse control
controls.body: Ten action keys and two ALT keys organize shortcuts by context. The encoder controls volume, scrolling or zoom depending on the layer; the joystick moves the pointer. USB and BLE send keyboard, mouse and media actions. WiFi is used for configuration and companion communication.

editor.title: Your configuration, without rebuilding
editor.body: The companion web editor changes layers, actions, text and macros, including Windows and Linux shortcut variants. It saves the editable configuration and sends the current operating system variant to PAD. A web mirror displays the device interface. Adapt the same hardware to editing, development, browsing or meetings.

companion.title: Real computer state
companion.body: The companion reads volume and microphone state, plus CPU/GPU load and temperature when sensors are available. It sends feedback to PAD over the local network and can toggle global microphone mute. Camera controls and some meeting shortcuts depend on the active application.

setup.title: Getting started
setup.body: Start with PAD over USB or BLE using its firmware layers. To add feedback and web editing, build the companion following its README, configure the PAD address and firmware-generated token, and run it on the same network. Windows includes login installation; Linux documents a systemd user service.

availability.title: What works independently
availability.body: HID shortcuts and controls work without a companion or WiFi. Real feedback and global microphone mute require the companion. Windows and Linux providers are implemented; macOS is not yet supported. Sensor readings depend on your hardware. Global camera mute is not implemented in the companion.

btdac.title: BTDAC: Bluetooth audio and test tools
btdac.description: BTDAC firmware receives Bluetooth audio and sends it to the PCM5102 DAC over I2S. A separate Android application connects over BLE to request test tones.

audio.title: From Bluetooth to your DAC
audio.body: The ESP32 acts as an A2DP receiver for audio from a phone or computer. RGB LEDs indicate waiting, connection, playback and errors. The BLE control channel is independent of the Bluetooth connection used for music.

android.title: Test tones from Android
android.body: The Kotlin application built with Jetpack Compose scans for the HIOS BTDAC BLE service, lets you select and connect a device, and sends frequency commands. Firmware generates stereo sine tones from 20 Hz to 20 kHz for approximately two seconds. It does not start a tone while music is playing.

setup.title: Getting started
setup.body: Build and flash the firmware following the BTDAC documentation. Pair an audio source to listen to music. For test tones, build the Android application from source, grant Bluetooth permissions and connect to BTDAC inside the application. No account or cloud service is required.

availability.title: Current scope
availability.body: The app lets you request test tones. Remote volume and equalization, battery monitoring and OTA updates are planned. The Android app is distributed as source code to build with Android Studio or Gradle.

0.body: HIOS brings together open hardware projects, documentation and development tools. Explore audio modules, programmable controls and examples that connect to local AI.

1.heading: Exploring the projects
1.body: Check the available features, requirements and planned work before building a device. Prototypes can change, so follow the instructions for the version you intend to use.

2.heading: Licenses
2.body: Check the license of each project and its dependencies before reusing code, designs or documentation.

3.heading: Contact

PrivacySettings.accountHint: Deleting your account removes its sessions, spaces, saved configurations, code snippets and preferences. Usage events and submitted messages remain without the account link; message content and contact emails are retained. Guestbook entries are also retained.
